abstract: We present the technical proposal for the Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE), a $\mathcal{O}(100)$ m vertical atom interferometer to be installed against the wall of the PX46 access shaft to the LHC. AICE is conceived as a versatile and flexible long-baseline atom-interferometry facility whose primary scientific goal is probing for bosonic ultralight dark matter (ULDM) in a mass range inaccessible to other experiments, with a secondary goal of pioneering the exploration of gravitational waves (GWs) with frequencies in the range ${\sim}$0.03-3 Hz as a pathfinder for future longer-baseline detectors. The initial configuration employs ultracold $^{87}$Sr atoms in a single-photon 698-nm interferometer with three shaft-based atom sources in a multi-source gradiometer geometry, supported by one surface reference source for laser stabilisation and diagnostics, to target scalar ULDM. Operation with $^{88}$Sr will give sensitivity to axion-like particles (ALPs), vector ULDM with $B-L$ couplings and violation of the principle of equivalence, while a $^{171}$Yb upgrade will improve the sensitivity to $B-L$ couplings and equivalence violations. Probing the Einstein equivalence principle (EP) and measuring $α$ will proceed in parallel with the ULDM searches. A conceptual feasibility study and a detailed technical implementation study have established that PX46 is a uniquely mature and implementation-ready site, with no technical showstoppers. Completing site preparation works during LS3 would enable the subsequent installation and operation of AICE without impacting HL-LHC operations. The detector design builds on the VLBAI and MAGIS experiments and the AION-10 Technical Design Report, scaling the strontium gradiometer architecture to the $\sim$100 m baseline. AICE is endorsed by the TVLBAI Proto-Collaboration, comprising 57 institutions in 22 countries.
summary: This technical proposal outlines the AICE facility, a large-scale atom interferometer planned for CERN to search for ultralight dark matter and test fundamental physics principles like the Equivalence Principle. By utilizing long baselines and various atomic species, it aims to achieve unprecedented precision in measuring fundamental constants and gravitational effects.
main_problem: The primary goal is probing for bosonic ultralight dark matter (ULDM) in a mass range inaccessible to other experiments, with a secondary goal of exploring gravitational waves (GWs) in the $\sim 0.03-3$ Hz range.
main_result: The proposal details the technical feasibility of the AICE facility, confirming that the PX46 site is mature and ready for installation to conduct these precision measurements.
method: The experiment uses long-baseline atom interferometry, employing ultracold atoms in a gradiometer geometry to measure phase shifts sensitive to external fields and fundamental constants.
model_or_system: The platform is the Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE), a $\mathcal{O}(100)$ m vertical interferometer utilizing ultracold $^{87}	ext{Sr}$ (with planned upgrades to $^{88}	ext{Sr}$ and $^{171}	ext{Yb}$) atoms.
key_observables: Dark matter coupling strengths, gravitational wave signals, violation of the Equivalence Principle (EP), and the fine-structure constant ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: Baseline length of $\sim 100$ m; GW frequency range of $\sim 0.03-3$ Hz; target sensitivity for $\alpha$ and EP violation.
main_assumptions: The proposal assumes the suitability and maturity of the PX46 site for installation without impacting LHC operations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides a general schematic view of AICE in the PX46 shaft, confirming compatibility with LHC component transport.
paper_structure: The proposal is structured to cover the motivation, the experimental concept (including gradiometer and multi-species operation), the detailed physics case (ULDM, $\alpha$, GWs), the technical detector systems, and the necessary site integration/civil engineering plans.
why_interesting: This work represents a major application of advanced cold atom techniques (atom interferometry) to fundamental physics, pushing the scale of terrestrial measurements significantly beyond current limits. It requires expertise in vacuum technology, laser cooling, and quantum sensing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Left panel: General schematic view of the proposed implementation of AICE in the PX46 access shaft [1, 2]. Right panel: Horizontal cross section of the PX46 shaft, showing that the proposed location of AICE (blue) is compatible with the space required for transport of LHC components (red hatched area).

Figure 2: Indicative timeline of the science programme for AICE from mid-2028 to the end of 2042, showing the main science phases, the atom species in use, the short precision physics campaigns embedded within each science phase, and the projected facility operating levels. Shutdowns for reconfiguration are indicated with grey background, and an optional future campaign is shown with a dashed border. Detailed descriptions of the operational phases are given in Section 8.

Figure 3: Left: a Mach-Zehnder optical interferometer. Right: the analogous atom inter- ferometer, with the ground state |g⟩represented by solid blue lines, the excited state |e⟩ by dashed red lines, and laser pulses by wavy lines. The π/2, π, π/2 pulse sequence acts as beamsplitter, mirror and beamsplitter respectively; the unlabelled rightmost pulse in the atom-interferometer schematic is the final π/2 beamsplitter pulse. Adapted from [51].

Figure 4: The transitions used for laser cooling and single-photon clock-transition interferom- etry in AICE. The long lifetimes of the 3P0 states in Sr [52] and Yb [53] suppress spontaneous- emission decoherence during the interferometer sequence. Indirect measurements of the Sr lifetime are in agreement with the direct measurement in Ref. [52] quoted here, but are in conflict with each other [55, 56].

Figure 5: Conceptual illustration of the multi-source facility architecture to be adopted by AICE. Left: the space-time diagram of one interferometer with n = 4 LMT momentum kicks. Right: several interferometers spaced within a single vertical vacuum tower of length L, forming multiple gradiometer combinations over different baselines. Multiple source stations permit simultaneous measurements over different baselines and provide a scalable architecture for future large-scale facilities. In AICE the number of sources grows from Nsource ∼3 at commissioning towards ∼10 to 20 at later stages (cf. Table 2). Adapted from [61].
